heuristics.rule: If multiple current students give evasive, defensive, or universally positive answers about their advisor, treat it as a negative signal — not a positive one
heuristics.condition: When conducting informational interviews with current PhD students during program visits or decision-making
heuristics.action: Weight generic praise and non-answers the same as negative signals; seek out specific, nuanced responses as the baseline for 'things are fine'
heuristics.because: People who are well-mentored give specific, detailed responses; uniformly positive or vague answers across multiple students indicate either fear of retaliation or coached responses

heuristics.rule: Ask about first-author publication counts by year 3–4 to detect advisor exploitation patterns
heuristics.condition: When evaluating an advisor who runs a large lab or whose own publication output is very high
heuristics.action: Ask current and former students how many first-author papers students typically have by years 3–4; compare across labs in the same field
heuristics.because: Exploiter advisors extract student labor for their own output while deprioritizing student authorship, leaving students with weak CVs relative to time invested — this pattern is directly detectable through publication data

heuristics.rule: If 3 or more of the last 8 students left a lab without finishing, do not treat this advisor as low-risk regardless of prestige
heuristics.condition: When researching a potential advisor's track record with previous students
heuristics.action: Count departures relative to total students mentored; a base rate of 37%+ departures is a structural signal about the advisor, not coincidence
heuristics.because: Individual incidents can be explained away; a pattern of departures reflects consistent conditions in the advising relationship that you are unlikely to be exempt from

heuristics.rule: When choosing between a known toxic advisor with high prestige and a good advisor with moderate prestige, default to the good advisor unless the prestige advantage is concretely quantifiable
heuristics.condition: When the research fit hierarchy leads you toward an advisor with a documented difficult reputation
heuristics.action: Verify whether 'their students get the jobs I want' is actually true — not just 'everyone says they're brilliant' — before weighting prestige advantage
heuristics.because: The worst-case outcome with a toxic advisor (leaving the field, lasting psychological harm) is substantially worse than the worst case with a good-enough advisor; the expected value calculation favors lower risk once worst-case is weighted appropriately

heuristics.rule: Ask 'What specifically needs to change for you to approve submission?' to diagnose a Perfectionist Blocker advisor
heuristics.condition: When a student's work is in extended revision with no clear completion criteria from the advisor
heuristics.action: Force the advisor to articulate concrete, satisfiable conditions for approval — or escalate to the Director of Graduate Studies
heuristics.because: Perfectionist Blockers operate by keeping criteria vague and perpetually raising the bar; making the conditions explicit either produces actionable feedback or exposes that the advisor has no clear threshold

heuristics.rule: Treat program attrition above 30% as requiring explicit explanation before accepting admission
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a PhD program's overall health and risk profile
heuristics.action: Ask the DGS directly about the attrition rate and its causes; compare to field averages; seek out former students who left
heuristics.because: High attrition reflects structural program conditions — advisor quality, funding precarity, culture — that will affect you regardless of your individual circumstances

decision_factors.factor: Advisor relationship quality and track record
decision_factors.why_it_matters: The advisor relationship is the single strongest predictor of PhD student mental health outcomes — stronger than funding, program rank, or research area; a toxic advisor compounds every other stressor in the program
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Interview current and former students in private settings; ask about responsiveness, emotional climate, publication authorship patterns, and student departure rates; look for specific vs. evasive answers

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Different advisor dysfunction patterns have different recovery potential; a Ghost advisor is more recoverable with co-advisor support than an Emotionally Volatile advisor, and an Exploiter damages career outcomes differently than a Perfectionist Blocker
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Map advisor behavior against specific patterns (Ghost, Perfectionist Blocker, Exploiter, Emotionally Volatile, Brilliant Jerk); ask former students directly about lab culture and what working with the advisor day-to-day is like

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A co-advisor, engaged DGS, formal mentoring committee, and collaborative lab culture can meaningfully buffer a difficult primary advisor; isolation amplifies advisor toxicity
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask whether co-advisors are available and used; assess whether DGS knows students by name and research area; evaluate whether formal mentoring committee meetings occur; ask about lab culture directly

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Funding contingent on advisor grants, competitive fellowship renewal, or TA position availability creates financial anxiety that compounds research anxiety; students with stable multi-year funding have one fewer major stressor
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask explicitly: Is funding guaranteed for the full program duration? What is the funding source — advisor grants, institutional fellowships, TA lines? What happens to funding if the advisor loses a grant?

decision_factors.factor: Program attrition rate and time-to-degree variance
decision_factors.why_it_matters: High attrition (above 30%) and wide time-to-degree variance signal advisor-dependent outcomes and structural program problems that affect all students
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the DGS for attrition data; look at time-to-degree distribution (not just average); speak with students in later years of the program about their progress trajectory

decision_factors.why_it_matters: Prestige is frequently cited as justification for accepting a difficult advisor, but the advantage is often based on reputation rather than actual placement outcomes — a mismatch that leads applicants to overweight prestige
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Check where the advisor's graduates from the last 5–7 years actually landed; verify whether those outcomes match your specific career goals; distinguish 'brilliant reputation' from 'students get the outcomes I want'

decision_factors.why_it_matters: An engaged Director of Graduate Studies who knows students by name and research area provides a meaningful escalation pathway and accountability check on advisor behavior; a purely administrative DGS leaves students without recourse
decision_factors.how_to_assess: During visits, observe whether the DGS references specific students by name; ask students whether they feel comfortable going to the DGS with problems; ask what happens when advisor-student relationships break down

decision_factors.factor: Availability of graduate-specific mental health resources
decision_factors.why_it_matters: General university counseling pools (shared with undergraduates) have long wait times and limited graduate student expertise; dedicated PhD counseling resources indicate institutional recognition of the structural problem
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask specifically whether there are graduate-student-only counseling slots, not just whether the university has a CAPS; ask current students whether they have used these resources and found them accessible

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing a high-prestige advisor with a known difficult reputation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The survival narratives from former students are selection-biased — only the people who survived are available to tell you it was worth it; the people who were most damaged by the experience left the field and are not in the room
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who rely heavily on testimonials and alumni networks to assess advisor risk; students from groups that the advisor has historically been more abusive toward

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Joining a large, highly productive lab
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Large labs increase Ghost and Exploiter risk — advisors are over-committed, and productive lab output may be driven by extracting student labor rather than developing individual students; first-author publication opportunities are diluted
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who join large labs expecting individualized mentorship comparable to smaller programs

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting funding that is contingent on advisor grants
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Research direction becomes constrained by whatever the advisor's grant covers, and a grant loss or advisor departure can create sudden funding crisis mid-program; the financial dependency compounds the evaluation dependency
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students who have no alternative income pathway and for whom funding loss creates both financial and visa status risk

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Entering a program with high attrition without investigating the cause
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: High attrition creates a cohort that progressively depletes of peers, eliminating the social and professional support networks that buffer mental health distress
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who rely on peer cohort for comparison, support, and collaboration — particularly those isolated from family networks

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Treating the PhD endpoint as undefined and managing it informally
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The chronic absence of clear progress milestones means distress can be misattributed to personal failure rather than structural training conditions, delaying recognition of advisor dysfunction or program problems
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: High-achieving students who have historically succeeded through individual effort and are predisposed to internalize struggle as personal inadequacy

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Prioritizing research fit and ranking over advisor mental health track record during program selection
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You are optimizing on observable, easily compared variables while systematically underweighting the single strongest predictor of your outcomes — advisor relationship quality — because it is harder to assess pre-enrollment
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: All applicants, but particularly those making decisions primarily from rankings, published research output, and lab websites rather than direct student interviews

failure_patterns.pattern: Evaluating programs on prestige, funding, and research fit while giving minimal attention to advisor mental health track record
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Prestige, funding amounts, and research fit are easily compared and publicly visible; advisor mental health track records require active investigation through private conversations, are rarely documented, and require asking uncomfortable questions
failure_patterns.consequence: Applicants optimize on observable variables while systematically underweighting the single strongest predictor of their PhD experience and completion outcomes
warning_signs: Decision rationale focuses primarily on lab publications, program rankings, and stipend comparisons
No direct private conversations with current students were conducted before accepting

failure_patterns.pattern: Interpreting survival narratives from successful PhD graduates as representative of the advisor experience
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Successful graduates are the only people available to give testimonials; those who left — often the most damaged — are not part of the professional network that applicants access during recruitment
failure_patterns.consequence: Applicants receive a heavily biased sample of advisor experience that overrepresents positive survivorship outcomes and leads to systematic underestimation of toxic advisor risk
warning_signs: All advisor references come from people who completed their PhDs and are now employed in the field
No attempt was made to contact students who left the program or left the advisor's lab

failure_patterns.pattern: Attributing slow progress and self-doubt to personal inadequacy rather than to structural advisor or program dysfunction
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: The chronic uncertainty of PhD training has no external benchmark; high-achieving students entering PhDs are accustomed to clear performance signals and have historically succeeded through individual effort, making internal attribution the default
failure_patterns.consequence: Students delay recognizing toxic advising patterns, do not escalate to DGS or seek support, and experience compounding psychological harm that could have been interrupted earlier
warning_signs: Student describes extensive self-doubt and lost confidence but attributes it entirely to their own capabilities
Student cannot identify any specific actionable feedback from advisor that would change their situation

failure_patterns.pattern: Using group visit conversations with current students as the primary source of social proof about advisor and program culture
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Group settings during recruitment visits feel like natural information-gathering opportunities; applicants don't realize that current students cannot speak honestly about advisors or program problems in group settings with faculty present or with peers who might report back
failure_patterns.consequence: Applicants receive only the public-facing, sanitized version of program culture and miss the signals that would be available in private one-on-one conversations
warning_signs: All student conversations during the visit occurred in group settings or in the presence of faculty
Applicant reports that 'everyone seemed happy and excited' with no more specific information

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating 'competitive culture' as a neutral or positive program descriptor without probing what it means in practice
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: High-achieving applicants often conflate competitive culture with high standards and excellence; the negative valence of competition in a constrained career environment is not salient until you are inside it
failure_patterns.consequence: Students enter environments with peer comparison dynamics, resource competition, and limited collaboration that compound the baseline mental health risks of PhD training
warning_signs: Program or students describe culture as 'competitive' without a positive counterbalance
No mention of collaborative structures, peer support mechanisms, or shared resources

diagnostic_questions.question: How do you feel about your progress day-to-day — not your research results, but your sense of whether you know what you're doing and where you're headed?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Distinguishes students with functional advising (who can articulate a sense of direction even amid uncertainty) from students experiencing Ghost or Perfectionist Blocker advising (who have chronic directionlessness or stuck-ness)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What does your advisor do that helps you maintain that sense of direction?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: How long have you felt that way, and what have you tried to address it?

diagnostic_questions.question: What do you do when you're having a hard week research-wise — is there a person you go to, and who is that?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the support structure exists and whether the advisor is accessible as a support resource; students with toxic advisors typically name peers, family, or external resources — not their advisor
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: How responsive is that person, and do you feel like you can bring real problems to them?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What has made it hard to find support within the program?

diagnostic_questions.question: Can you tell me about a student who left the program or left this lab in the last few years — what happened to them?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Directly accesses departure information and tests whether the culture treats attrition as discussable or as a taboo topic; evasion or dismissal of this question is itself a signal
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Was their experience typical, or was it unusual compared to most students here?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Is that something people don't really talk about here?

diagnostic_questions.question: How many first-author papers have students in this lab typically published by the time they're in year 3 or 4?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Assesses exploitation pattern risk; very low first-author counts relative to program duration and lab output volume indicate students are contributing to advisor publications without receiving authorship credit
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: What does the process look like from project idea to publication — how involved is the advisor at each stage?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What are students working on that isn't getting published yet?

diagnostic_questions.question: Have you ever used the counseling or mental health resources at the university — were they useful and accessible for grad students specifically?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Normalizes mental health discussion, reveals whether students have needed support (base rate indicator), and tests whether the university's resources are actually grad-student-accessible or theoretically available but practically inaccessible
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Were there dedicated slots for grad students or did you compete with undergrads for appointments?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Do you know if other students have used them? Is it something people talk about here?

diagnostic_questions.question: What would you do if you had a serious conflict with your advisor — is there a clear path you'd take?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Tests whether the escalation pathway (DGS, ombudsperson, mentoring committee) is real and known to students or theoretical and unknown; students in functional departments can describe the path clearly
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Have you seen that path actually work for someone?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: Does that feel like something you'd be comfortable doing, or does it seem risky to use those resources?

diagnostic_questions.question: Is the advisor's prestige advantage reflected in actual placement data — where have their students from the last 5–7 years actually ended up?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Distinguishes real prestige advantage (students consistently get desired outcomes) from reputation prestige (advisor is considered brilliant but student placement is not systematically better than good-enough alternatives)
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: Are those the specific types of positions and organizations I'm targeting?
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: What explains the gap between the advisor's reputation and the placement outcomes?

industry_realities.common_belief: Mental health struggles during a PhD are caused by individual weakness, impostor syndrome, or poor personal coping — they are the exception, not the rule
industry_realities.actual_reality: Mental health distress is a structural feature of PhD training, not an individual failure: 36% of PhD students seek help for anxiety or depression related to their PhD, and PhD students are 2.43x more likely to experience depression and anxiety than similarly-educated comparison groups
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should treat mental health risk as a program selection variable to be actively assessed — not as a personal contingency to manage after enrollment

industry_realities.common_belief: The advisor relationship is one of several factors affecting PhD quality, roughly comparable in importance to program ranking, research fit, and funding
industry_realities.actual_reality: The advisor relationship is the single strongest predictor of PhD student mental health outcomes — stronger than funding, program rank, or research area; 43% of students with negative or unsupportive advisors met criteria for moderate-severe anxiety
industry_realities.implication: Advisor assessment deserves disproportionate weight in program selection decisions relative to the attention most applicants give it

industry_realities.common_belief: Surviving a tough advisor is a rite of passage that builds resilience and is widely validated by successful people in the field
industry_realities.actual_reality: Survival narratives are selection-biased: only the people who survived are available to describe the experience; the people most damaged by toxic advisors left the field and are absent from the professional networks that applicants consult
industry_realities.implication: Positive testimonials about difficult advisors should be discounted for survivorship bias; applicants should specifically seek out information about students who left the lab or program

industry_realities.common_belief: A PhD program with high output, prestigious publications, and strong placement statistics is a well-functioning program with good advising
industry_realities.actual_reality: High lab output and strong placement statistics can coexist with Exploiter advising patterns; aggregate program prestige metrics do not differentiate between advisors who develop students and advisors who extract student labor while producing strong lab-level outcomes
industry_realities.implication: Program-level metrics must be disaggregated to the advisor level to be useful for predicting individual student experience

industry_realities.common_belief: University counseling services are available and accessible to PhD students who need support
industry_realities.actual_reality: Most universities have general CAPS services that share capacity with the undergraduate population, creating long wait times and limited graduate-student-specific expertise; dedicated PhD counseling slots are an indicator of institutional seriousness about the problem, not a universal baseline
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should explicitly verify whether graduate-specific counseling slots exist — not just whether a university has a counseling center

industry_realities.common_belief: If students were experiencing serious problems with an advisor, they would use formal escalation pathways like the DGS or ombudsperson
industry_realities.actual_reality: Emotionally volatile and abusive advisors create hypervigilance and avoidance of bringing problems forward; students often do not escalate because they fear retaliation, do not know the pathways exist, or have internalized the dysfunction as their own failure
industry_realities.implication: The absence of reported problems or formal complaints about an advisor should not be interpreted as evidence that no problems exist

industry_realities.common_belief: Wide variation in time-to-degree across a program reflects different research topics requiring different amounts of time
industry_realities.actual_reality: Wide time-to-degree distribution (some finishing in 4 years, others taking 8–10) primarily signals advisor-dependent outcomes rather than research complexity; students under Ghost or Perfectionist Blocker advisors accumulate years without making completion progress
industry_realities.implication: Time-to-degree variance is a diagnostic indicator of advisor quality distribution within a program, not just a research complexity artifact

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Focuses on program rankings, lab publication output, advisor reputation, and funding amount — all externally visible and easily compared metrics
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Weights advisor-specific track record with students (departure rates, authorship patterns, student mental health outcomes) above aggregate program prestige; investigates what is not visible on the program website
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Optimizing on visible metrics while ignoring the strongest predictor of outcomes (advisor relationship) leads to systematically poor program selection decisions

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Relies on published work, citation counts, field reputation, and testimonials from successful graduates; treats consensus 'brilliant' reputation as sufficient positive signal
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Distinguishes 'brilliant researcher' from 'effective mentor'; actively seeks information about students who left the lab; asks for concrete placement outcomes rather than general reputation claims; checks for patterns across student types
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Brilliant researcher and effective mentor are independent dimensions; conflating them leads applicants to accept toxic advising situations that their field reputation does not justify

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Takes positive student feedback at face value; interprets enthusiasm and generic praise as evidence of program quality; conducts information gathering in group visit settings
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Seeks private one-on-one conversations; reads evasiveness and universal positivity as negative signals; asks specific behavioral questions rather than opinion questions; accounts for selection bias in who is available to give testimonials
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Public-facing testimonials systematically omit the information most relevant to assessing advisor toxicity; failing to access private signals leads to decisions based on curated information

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to think about worst-case scenarios
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Focuses on expected-case outcomes — 'if things go well, I'll get X'; discounts worst-case scenarios as unlikely or manageable through personal effort
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Explicitly models worst-case outcomes and weights them by probability; recognizes that the worst case with a toxic advisor (leaving field, lasting psychological harm) is categorically worse than worst case with a good advisor; uses asymmetry of outcomes as a decision input
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Expected value calculations that ignore worst-case scenarios systematically overvalue high-upside/high-risk options; the PhD context has unusually severe downside risk that needs explicit weighting

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How mental health risk is treated in the decision
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats mental health as a personal management challenge to address after enrollment if needed; does not include it as a program selection variable; assumes personal resilience will compensate for structural risk
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats mental health risk as a structural feature of PhD training that must be priced into program selection; actively investigates advisor and program mental health track record before accepting; treats attrition rates and support structures as primary decision inputs
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Entering a high-risk advising environment without assessment, on the assumption that personal resilience will compensate, is the most common path to the worst-case outcome

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: How to interpret the 'competitive culture' descriptor
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Associates competitive culture with high standards and high-achieving peers; treats it as a positive signal about program quality and the caliber of colleagues
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Probes what competitive culture means in practice — resource competition, peer comparison dynamics, limited collaboration, absence of mutual support — and weights it as a mental health risk factor in an already high-distress environment
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Competitive culture in a constrained academic job market context amplifies comparison dynamics and compounds baseline PhD mental health risk; treating it as a positive without interrogating the mechanism leads to environment underestimation
